name: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
title: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
answer: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of having a language model answer legal questions only from documents that have been fetched and cited, rather than from whatever the model absorbed during training. In case strategy it covers finding controlling authority, checking that a cited case still says what it is claimed to say, tracing how a rule has been applied across jurisdictions, and assembling a record of sources a supervising lawyer can review. It sits alongside traditional database search rather than replacing it, and it is most useful where the volume of material is large and the cost of a missed or misstated authority is high.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of having a language model answer legal questions only from documents that have been fetched and cited, rather than from whatever the model absorbed during training. In case strategy it covers finding controlling authority, checking that a cited case still says what it is claimed to say, tracing how a rule has been applied across jurisdictions, and assembling a record of sources a supervising lawyer can review. It sits alongside traditional database search rather than replacing it, and it is most useful where the volume of material is large and the cost of a missed or misstated authority is high.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The system runs on a retrieval layer and a generation layer that are kept separate. The retrieval layer indexes the firm's own matter files, licensed case law and statute databases, and public sources, usually through a vector store for semantic matching plus keyword search for exact citations and docket numbers. The generation layer is a hosted or self-hosted language model that receives the retrieved passages as context and is instructed to answer only from them. Access control, audit logging, and a snapshot of the index at the time of the query are part of the infrastructure, because a citation that cannot be reproduced later is of little use in a filing.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts by turning a legal question into a set of retrievable queries, which often means decomposing it into jurisdiction, cause of action, procedural posture, and date range. Retrieved passages are ranked and filtered, then passed to the model with instructions to quote and cite, and the output is checked back against the source text before anyone relies on it. A competent workflow treats every generated citation as unverified until a human or a separate verification step confirms the case exists, is still good law, and supports the proposition. Where the corpus is thin or the question is novel, the honest output is a statement that the retrieved material does not answer it.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are fabricated or misattributed authority, outdated law, privileged material leaking into a third-party model, and confidentiality obligations that follow the documents wherever they go. Provenance is the control: each answer should carry the source, the version retrieved, the date, and the person who reviewed it, so that a later challenge can be met with a record rather than a recollection. Courts have begun to treat unverified AI-assisted filings as a professional responsibility problem, and the site's tracking of 150 active AI lawsuits and 29 AI case law precedents reflects how quickly that body of practice is forming. Licensing terms for the underlying databases also constrain what can be indexed, stored, or shown to a client.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect retrieval grounding to become the default posture for any legal AI tool that touches authority, with verification moving from a manual afterthought to an enforced step in the pipeline. Citation-level checks against official reporters, jurisdiction-aware routing, and audit trails that survive a motion to strike are the likely areas of refinement. The harder problems are not technical: they are who bears responsibility when a grounded system still returns a bad source, and how firms document that a human read the result. As state and federal rules continue to accumulate, the practical dividing line will be between tools that can show their work and tools that cannot.
